design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, two-period crossover study with counterbalanced and sex-balanced order: 16 healthy adults who had rarely or never used GHB took one oral dose of pharmaceutical GHB (sodium oxybate, Xyrem) and, on another day, a taste-matched placebo, then drove a validated simulator before dosing and three times after it on an inpatient research unit in San Francisco, with blood GHB measured before each drive and self-rated ability to drive.
can_establish: How much one laboratory dose of GHB worsened simulated driving and self-rated ability to drive at the first drive after dosing in people who had rarely or never used GHB, whether those measures still differed detectably from placebo at the two later drives the same day, and how blood GHB related to driving errors at the first drive.
cannot_establish: Driving in real traffic; effects in people who use GHB regularly (tolerance), who redose or who combine GHB with alcohol or other drugs; effects of other doses; that driving was safe at the later drives (absence of a detectable difference in 16 people is not evidence of no impairment, and the four people most affected were excluded); and effects the morning after a night-time dose, which was not tested.

sample.recruitment: Newspaper and online advertisements and flyers in San Francisco Bay Area cafes and colleges; telephone then in-person screening with medical history, physical examination, blood tests and urine toxicology (Methods › Recruitment).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Ages 21 to 45, valid driver's licence, GHB-naive or at most occasional use (fewer than three times a year), no prescription medicines other than contraceptives. Excluded: significant medical conditions, pregnancy, body mass index 30 or more, substance use or prescription drugs that could not be stopped for two weeks before the study, and more than 5 alcoholic drinks a week.
sample.demographics: Mean age 27 (range 22 to 42); mean weight 69.1 kg; 8 women and 8 men; 2 of 16 reported past GHB use (Results › Demographics).
sample.attrition: Four men vomited after GHB and could not complete the first post-dose drive; they were replaced by four new men and are not in the results. Only the 16 who completed every part were analysed.
sample.selection_effects: Healthy, light-drinking, mostly GHB-naive volunteers with intensive simulator training; people who use GHB recreationally, often with alcohol and repeated doses, were excluded by design. Excluding the four who became too ill to drive removes the most affected participants from the first post-dose comparison.

exposure.measurement: Randomized administration of oral GHB or matched placebo on two inpatient study days; blood GHB by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry before dosing and before each post-dose drive.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: one oral dose of GHB 50 mg per kg body weight (Xyrem, dosed as GHB), mixed with cranberry or orange juice, at 9 am after a light breakfast; the four replacement men had the dose capped at 3300 mg, so the lowest dose was 45 mg/kg; mean dose 3333 mg (SD 400, range 2892 to 4265). Baseline drive at 8 am, post-dose drives at 1, 3 and 6 hours after dosing (10 am, noon, 3 pm), each 18 to 20 minutes. Median plasma GHB 83.1 mg/L (range 54 to 110) at 1 hour and 24.4 mg/L (7.2 to 49.7) at 3 hours; not detectable at baseline or 6 hours (limit of quantitation 5 mg/L). The two arms were separated by at least one night (one to six days in eight participants). Alcohol avoided for three days before each study day; overnight fast without caffeine or tobacco.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable: other drugs, alcohol, caffeine and tobacco were restricted before and during study days; urine toxicology at screening.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (acute and same-day residual effects of one study dose).

comparison.controls: The same participants after taste-matched placebo on another study day (within-person crossover).
comparison.matching: Within-person comparison; order counterbalanced and sex-balanced; baseline drives did not differ between the two study days.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable for a within-person randomized comparison; sleep the night before each study day was spent on the unit but not measured.

outcomes.instruments: Systems Technology driving simulator (three screens, urban, suburban and rural segments, about 12 miles) previously validated in alcohol studies: collisions, off-road accidents, pedestrian hits, speeding and traffic-light tickets, stops at lights, mean speed and its standard deviation, speed exceedances, mean lane position and its standard deviation, and a divided-attention task (correct, incorrect and missed responses, response time and its variability); a 1 to 5 self-rating of ability to drive before each drive.
outcomes.validity_norms: The simulator had been used to grade impairment by alcohol (Moskowitz 2000); the comparison of the GHB effect with breath-alcohol levels is made against that earlier study, not measured here.
outcomes.operationalization: Collisions, off-road accidents and pedestrian hits are classed as life-threatening outcomes; speed and lane-position variability as driving style.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; the authors note that the main findings remain significant at p < 0.01 and have large effect sizes. The 64 counts 15 simulator outcomes and the self-rating at four drives, before within-arm and correlation tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Simulator outcomes were scored automatically. Participants and staff were blind in design, but the sedation and nausea GHB causes make unblinding likely, which matters most for the self-ratings.

analysis.effect_sizes: Within-person Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with effect size r = Z divided by the square root of 32 observations. First post-dose drive, GHB against placebo: collisions median 6.5 (range 2 to 19) against 1 (0 to 4), Z = -3.526, p < 0.001, r = -0.62, more collisions after GHB in all 16; off-road accidents median 0 (0 to 7) against 0 (0 to 2), Z = -2.375, p = 0.018, r = -0.42, more in 7 participants and fewer in none; speed deviation 4.09 against 2.76, Z = -3.051, p = 0.002, r = -0.54, greater in 13 of 16; lane-position deviation 1.93 against 1.23, Z = -2.896, p = 0.004, r = -0.51, greater in 13 of 16; mean speed and pedestrian hits not significant. Second post-dose drive: no simulator outcome differed; self-rated ability still lower after GHB (p = 0.001), with nearly a third rating themselves 3 or worse on the 5-point scale. Third post-dose drive: no simulator or self-rating difference except greater speed deviation after placebo (Z = -2.279, p = 0.017, r = -0.42). Spearman correlations at the first drive between plasma GHB and lane-position deviation r = 0.532 and speed deviation r = 0.588 (both p < 0.05).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No trial registration or protocol is cited in the article.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 15 simulator outcomes are tabulated at all four drives with medians, ranges and p values, which limits selective reporting; there is no correction for multiple comparisons.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation reported; 16 participants give little power to detect smaller residual impairment at the later drives.

interpretation_gap.results_show: At the first drive after a single laboratory dose, every participant had more simulator collisions than after placebo (median 6.5 against 1), with more off-road accidents and more weaving in speed and lane position, and all rated themselves less able to drive. At the two later drives the same day no simulator measure was worse than after placebo, but at the middle drive people still rated themselves less able to drive. Blood GHB at the first drive correlated with weaving.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that after three to six hours there was full recovery, indicating that safe driving is expected the next morning after bedtime therapeutic GHB use without other substances; the discussion adds that daytime driving restrictions are not indicated for people with narcolepsy who take GHB at night. Gaps: (1) ‘full recovery’ rests on non-significant differences in 16 people, after excluding the four who were too ill to drive; (2) night-time dosing, sleep and morning driving were not studied, nor the second nightly dose used in narcolepsy; (3) the participants had rarely or never used GHB and took no alcohol, so the results do not transfer to recreational use with redosing or alcohol, which the authors acknowledge; (4) the equivalence of the first-drive impairment to a breath-alcohol range is a comparison with another study, not a measurement here. The authors' own closing caution, that driving within a few hours of use may be hazardous, follows the data.

timeline.event: This study: described by its authors as the first controlled study of GHB on simulated driving.
Centola et al. review of GHB and driving performance (as cited by this paper), which reports no other real-driving or simulator studies.
Van Amsterdam et al. systematic review of cognition after GHB use; this driving study is not among its acute human studies

replication.where_it_stands: The only controlled simulator study of GHB in the papers read for this card. Its first-drive impairment is large and consistent across participants; its later-drive results show no detectable impairment in a small, naive sample and have not been repeated, nor tested after night-time dosing, at other doses or with alcohol.

funding.funder: National Center for Research Resources (NIH) and NIH Roadmap for Medical Research grants MO1RR00083-44 and UL1 RR024131-01; NIDA grants DA14935 and DA12393.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors have no conflicts to disclose.
funding.affiliations_note: The study was approved by the University of California, San Francisco and run at Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital; author affiliations were not expanded in the page text read. The study medicine was the marketed product (Xyrem); no manufacturer funding is stated.

what_would_settle_it: A placebo-controlled crossover study in people who use GHB recreationally and in people taking it at night for narcolepsy, testing on-road or simulator driving at several times after dosing, including the next morning after a night-time dose and after GHB with alcohol, powered to show equivalence with placebo rather than only a lack of significant difference.

domains.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
domains.note: Order randomized, counterbalanced and sex-balanced; the method of sequence generation and concealment is not described. Baseline drives did not differ between study days.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Double-blind with taste-matched placebo, but GHB's sedative and gastrointestinal effects make unblinding likely; the dose was capped for the four replacement participants.

domains.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
domains.note: Four of the 20 people who took GHB (all men) vomited and could not drive after it; they were replaced and excluded. Their missing data were caused by the intervention and relate to the outcome.

domains.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Simulator outcomes are recorded automatically and do not depend on the assessor; the self-ratings are open to expectation effects.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No registered protocol cited; all outcomes are tabulated at all drives, but there is no correction for about 64 comparisons.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: One domain is high (replacement and exclusion of the four participants who became too ill to drive after GHB), so the overall judgment is high under RoB 2. The bias runs towards underestimating impairment at the first drive and towards overstating recovery later, so the first-drive impairment is, if anything, conservative. Carry-over is unlikely given GHB's short half-life and at least a night between arms; practice effects were reduced by extensive training and counterbalancing. The study may be cited for marked impairment of simulated driving at the first drive after one laboratory dose in GHB-naive adults and for the absence of a detectable difference at the two later drives in completers; it should not be cited as showing that driving is safe at any time after GHB, for regular use, or for GHB with alcohol.

key_findings.finding: At the first drive after GHB, every one of the 16 participants had more simulator collisions than after placebo: median 6.5 (range 2 to 19) against 1 (0 to 4); Z = -3.526, p < 0.001, r = -0.62. Off-road accidents also increased (Z = -2.375, p = 0.018, r = -0.42; more in 7 participants, fewer in none); pedestrian hits did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Results › Driving Questionnaire and Simulator results, 3rd paragraph; Table 2, No. of collisions and No. of off road accidents rows

key_findings.finding: At the first drive after GHB, driving was more erratic without being faster: speed deviation 4.09 against 2.76 (Z = -3.051, p = 0.002, r = -0.54; greater in 13 of 16) and lane-position deviation 1.93 against 1.23 (Z = -2.896, p = 0.004, r = -0.51; greater in 13 of 16); mean speed did not differ (50 against 52 mph, p = 0.12).
key_findings.locator: Results › Driving Questionnaire and Simulator results, 3rd paragraph; Table 2, Mean speed, Mean speed deviation and Mean lane position deviation rows

key_findings.finding: Self-rated ability to drive was worse after GHB at the first drive in all participants (median 4 against 1 on a 1 to 5 scale, p < 0.001) and still worse at the second drive (p = 0.001), when nearly a third of ratings were 3 or higher; at the third drive it no longer differed.
key_findings.locator: Results › Driving Questionnaire and Simulator results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 legend

key_findings.finding: At the second and third drives after GHB, no simulator outcome was worse than after placebo (Table 2); at the third drive speed deviation was greater after placebo (Z = -2.279, p = 0.017). Within the GHB arm, collisions, off-road accidents, speed deviation and lane-position deviation at the first drive were all worse than at baseline and at the two later drives.
key_findings.locator: Results › Driving Questionnaire and Simulator results, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 2
key_findings.note: Z = -2.279 corresponds to a two-sided normal-approximation p of about 0.023, not 0.017 (editors' calculation); the reported p may come from an exact test.

key_findings.finding: Plasma GHB at the first drive correlated with lane-position deviation (r = 0.532) and speed deviation (r = 0.588), both p < 0.05; correlations with the other driving outcomes were not significant. Plasma levels did not differ between women and men (p = 0.208).
key_findings.locator: Results › GHB dosing, blood concentrations, and correlations, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Four men vomited after GHB and could not complete the first post-dose drive; they were replaced, the dose was capped for the replacements, and only the 16 who completed every session were analysed.
key_findings.locator: Methods › GHB and Placebo Dosing, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors list as limitations one dose only (adjusted for four participants), no people who use GHB regularly (possible tolerance), practice effects on the simulator (reduced by training and counterbalancing) and no correction for multiple comparisons.

reporting_issues.issue: The off-road accident result is printed as p<0.018 in the Results text and as p = 0.018 in the abstract and Table 2.
The Discussion gives the plasma GHB level at the last drive as below a limit one-tenth of the limit of quantitation stated in the Results (recorded in the exposure field).
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two limits is a typographical error; either way GHB was not detectable at the last drive.

reporting_issues.issue: For greater speed deviation after placebo at the third drive, Z = -2.279 is printed with p = 0.017; the normal approximation gives about 0.023 (editors' calculation), while the other Z and p pairs agree.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the finding is an incidental difference favouring GHB and does not affect the conclusions.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's conclusion about safe driving the next morning after bedtime use extrapolates to a dosing schedule (night-time doses with sleep) that the study did not test.
reporting_issues.consequence: The next-morning statement is an inference, not a finding; claims should report only the same-day daytime results.
